claims.claim: When persecuted for your faith, it is right to flee if you can.

stances.summary: Flight in persecution is permitted, and it is better to flee from town to town than to be caught and deny Christ. But it is only a concession. Those who stand and confess are more blessed.
stances.quote: Why, even in persecutions it is better to take advantage of the permission granted, and flee from town to town, than, when apprehended and racked, to deny (the faith). And therefore more blessed are they who have strength to depart (this life) in blessed confession of their testimony.
stances.original: Etiam in persecutionibus melius ex permissu fugere de oppido in oppidum, quam comprehensum et distortum negare. At quanto beatiores, qui ualent beata testimonii confessione excedere.
stances.context: EARLIER VIEW, before his Montanist years (To His Wife is usually dated about 200-206). The line is an analogy inside an argument about remarriage: marriage, like flight, is a permitted lesser good, and what is merely permitted "is not good" in the full sense. So even here flight is second best. The parentheses are the translator's. Latin checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.uxor1.shtml (section 3.4). About a decade later he reversed himself completely in On Flight in Persecution (next entry), without acknowledging the earlier permission.

stances.summary: Persecution comes by God's will to test faith, so running from it is running from God. Only fear makes a person flee, and fear shows a lack of love. The command to flee in Matthew 10 was for the apostles' mission to Israel only, and it has lapsed. Clergy who flee are the hireling who leaves the sheep. Paying bribes to escape is flight with money and just as wrong.
stances.quote: And yet who will flee from persecution, but he who fears? Who will fear, but he who has not loved?
stances.original: Porro quis fugiet persecutionem, nisi qui timebit? quis timebit, nisi qui non amabit?
stances.work: On Flight in Persecution (De fuga in persecutione)
stances.context: LATER VIEW. The whole treatise (about 208-212, his Montanist period) answers a friend, Fabius, who asked "whether or not we ought to flee in persecution"; chapter 4 concludes "that men should not flee in it." Other blunt lines: "It beseems us better to retain our position in submission to the will of God, than to flee at our own will" (ch. 5); "He who fears to suffer, cannot belong to Him who suffered" (ch. 14; Latin "Non potest, qui pati timet, ei esse, qui passus est"). He reads Matthew 10:23 as limited to the apostles' first mission (ch. 6), and in chapter 11 says it is "absolutely unlawful" for "deacons, and presbyters, and bishops" to flee. He leans openly on Montanist prophecy: he quotes an oracle of "the Spirit" urging believers "to die the martyr's death" (ch. 9) and says those who have received the Paraclete "will neither stoop to flee from persecution nor to buy it off" (ch. 14). Heterodox: he joined the Montanists and is not venerated as a saint. This reverses his earlier permission in To His Wife 1.3 (previous entry). Latin checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.fuga.shtml.

stances.summary: Christ's command to flee is not about fear of death. It is about not making ourselves guilty. Whoever walks into the court and hands himself over shares in the persecutor's crime. Take care of yourself, and do not provoke.
stances.quote: For He, in a way, bids us take care of ourselves. But he who disobeys is rash and foolhardy. If he who kills a man of God sins against God, he also who presents himself before the judgment-seat becomes guilty of his death.
stances.context: The chapter is headed in ANF "Those Who Offered Themselves for Martyrdom Reproved". It opens with Matthew 10:23 and says Christ "does not advise flight, as if persecution were an evil thing; nor does He enjoin them by flight to avoid death, as if in dread of it". So his reason for fleeing is moral, not self-protective: not to become "an accomplice in the crime of the persecutor". Book 4 chapter 4 adds that those "in haste to give themselves up" (he names heretics "dying through hatred to the Creator") "banish themselves without being martyrs". He still praises true martyrdom at length in the same book. Written about 200-202. Clement seems to have left Alexandria himself in the persecution under Severus (Eusebius, Church History 6.3, says teachers were "driven away by the threat of persecution"), but that is not in his own words. Never formally condemned, though not generally venerated as a saint in the West.

stances.summary: Where you can avoid persecution, avoid it. That is prudence, and walking into danger you could escape is rash. Where you cannot avoid it, endure it with courage. When a Christian flees, it is obedience to Christ, not cowardice, so that he can go on helping others.
stances.quote: When a temptation comes which is not in our power to avoid, we must endure it with exceeding nobleness and courage; but, when it is in our power to avoid it, not to do so is rash.
stances.location: book 10, section 23 ("The Withdrawal of Jesus", on Matthew 14:13)
stances.context: Just before: "The letter teaches us to withdraw as far as it is in our power from those who persecute us ... when one can keep outside of critical positions, to go to meet them is rash and headstrong," and he cites Matthew 10:23. Written about 246-248. He says the same in Against Celsus 8.44 (ANF 4): "If a Christian ever flees away, it is not from fear, but in obedience to the command of his Master, that so he may preserve himself, and employ his strength for the benefit of others"; and in 1.65 he says Jesus taught His disciples "not to be guilty of rashness" and did not "expose Himself to danger rashly". Contrast with his youth: Eusebius (Church History 6.2) says the teenage Origen was so eager for martyrdom when his father was arrested (202) that his mother hid all his clothes to keep him home. That is Eusebius's report, not Origen's own statement of principle, so it is not entered as a separate stance. He was himself tortured in the Decian persecution and died soon after. Some of his speculative teachings were condemned long after his death (553); he is not venerated as a saint.

stances.summary: The Lord commanded us to withdraw and flee in persecution, and did it Himself. Confessing before the judge is the first crown. Withdrawing in secret so as not to deny Him is the second. What is wrong is staying put and then denying.
stances.quote: And therefore the Lord commanded us in the persecution to depart and to flee; and both taught that this should be done, and Himself did it.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.original: Et ideo Dominus in persecutione secedere et fugere mandavit, atque, ut id fieret, et docuit et fecit.
stances.context: Written in 251, after the Decian persecution, during which Cyprian had himself hidden outside Carthage and was criticised for it. Section 3: "It is the first title to victory to confess the Lord under the violence of the hands of the Gentiles. It is the second step to glory to be withdrawn by a cautious retirement, and to be reserved for the Lord." Section 10 continues: "whosoever abiding in Christ departs for a while does not deny his faith, but waits for the time; but he who has fallen, after refusing to depart, remained to deny it." In his letters he says he withdrew "taking into consideration not so much my own safety as the public peace of the brethren" (Epistle 14 in ANF numbering). To the people of Thibaris (Epistle 55 ANF) he writes of believers who scatter: "He is not alone, whose companion in flight Christ is". He also forbade volunteering: in his last letter (Epistle 82 ANF, 258) he tells his people not to "voluntarily offer himself to the Gentiles". In 258 he refused friends' offers of hiding places (Pontius, Life 14) and hid only briefly so as to be tried in Carthage, among his own people, rather than at Utica. That is not a change of principle: he held there is a time to withdraw and a time to confess. Latin checked at https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/De_lapsis.

stances.summary: Cyprian did not hide out of fear. He hid because the Lord told him to, and because the Church needed him alive. His later martyrdom proves it.
stances.quote: For a mind dedicated in all things to God, and thus enslaved to the divine admonitions, believed that even in suffering itself it would sin, unless it had obeyed the Lord, who then bade him seek the place of concealment.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Pontius was Cyprian's deacon and companion in exile; he wrote soon after Cyprian's death in 258. Not in the results pool. Just before the quote: "Do you wish to be assured that the cause of his withdrawal was not fear? To allege nothing else, he did suffer subsequently". Chapter 8 argues the withdrawal "was not conceived by human pusillanimity" but "was truly divine", because it preserved the man the Church needed. Chapter 14 records that in 258 Cyprian refused friends who "repeatedly urged his withdrawal" and offered places to hide, adding that he might have gone "if it had been bidden him by divine command".

stances.summary: I fled in the Decian persecution, but not on my own impulse. God told me to go, and the good that came of it shows it was His doing.
stances.quote: I speak before God, and he knows that I do not lie. I did not flee on my own impulse nor without divine direction.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter to Germanus (quoted by Eusebius, Church History)
stances.location: Eusebius, Church History 6.40.1 (more of the same letter at 7.11)
stances.context: Bishop of Alexandria (died about 264); not in the results pool. Written about 259-260 to answer Germanus, a fellow bishop who accused him of cowardly flight. He says he first stayed at home four days while he was searched for, "and after the fourth day God commanded me to depart". His own words survive only as quoted by Eusebius (early 4th century). So his defence rests on divine direction in his case, not on a general rule; he also records confessing openly before the prefect Aemilianus in 257 (7.11). The lower-case "he" for God is the translator's.

stances.summary: Christ said they will hand you over, not that you should hand yourselves over. He wants us to move from place to place while we are hunted, and not to provoke the persecutors into more killing. No one may blame those who left everything and fled to save their lives.
stances.quote: for He would have us pass from place to place as long as there are those who persecute us for His name's sake; even as again we hear Him saying, But when they persecute you in this city, flee into another.
stances.translation: James B. H. Hawkins, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6, 1886
stances.context: Bishop of Alexandria, written about 306 during the Great Persecution; he was himself martyred in 311. Not in the results pool. Canon 9 deals with those who "themselves leap forth upon a contest": the Church still communicates with them, but they ignored the prayer "lead us not into temptation", and he notes that the Lord "often retired from those who would lay snares for Him" and "delivered not up Himself". Canon 13: "neither is it lawful to accuse those who have left all, and have retired for the safety of their life, as if Others had been held back by them" (the capital O is in the page). These canons were later received into Eastern church law (the page includes the Byzantine commentators Balsamon and Zonaras).

stances.summary: Scripture gives everyone a law: flee when persecuted, hide when hunted, and do not rashly tempt God. Jacob, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul and Christ Himself all fled. Flight is not cowardice. When the hour truly comes, you meet death without shrinking.
stances.quote: And to all men generally, even to us, is this law given, to flee when persecuted, and to hide when sought after, and not rashly tempt the Lord
stances.translation: M. Atkinson and Archibald Robertson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Defence of His Flight (Apologia de fuga)
stances.context: A whole treatise (about 357) answering Arian bishops who mocked him as a coward for escaping when soldiers stormed his church in Alexandria in 356. Chapter 22 goes on: "When persecuted they fled, while concealing themselves they showed fortitude, and when discovered they submitted to martyrdom." Chapter 23: "Our Lord commanded to flee, and the saints fled". Chapter 17 says that to offer oneself up without reason "would have been to kill themselves", and that those who died in flight still "attained ... the glory of martyrdom". He allows that some saints did present themselves, but only when moved by the Spirit (ch. 17, 22). He spent years hiding, some of them among the desert monks. Augustine later cites his flight as the model of a rightful one (Letter 228).

stances.summary: I will not hand myself over, but I will not hide either. I go where the martyrs are, to stand by them, and if I am called I will fight.
stances.quote: Let us go too, that if called, we may contend or behold them that are contending. And he longed to suffer martyrdom, but not being willing to give himself up, he ministered to the confessors in the mines and in the prisons.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Athanasius knew Antony and wrote the Life soon after his death (about 357-362). The first sentence is Antony's own recorded words, the second Athanasius's narration. Setting: the persecution under Maximinus (about 311). When the judge ordered all monks out of the city, "all the rest thought it good to hide themselves that day", but Antony washed his garment and stood all next day on a raised place in full view of the governor, "showing the readiness of us Christians". He grieved that he was not martyred. So he neither volunteered nor hid; the Life does not blame those who hid. Entered as mixed because his own conduct was to stay visible rather than flee, while keeping the rule against giving oneself up.

stances.summary: The law of martyrdom forbids two things: rushing to meet it, which is foolhardy, and shrinking from it when it comes, which is cowardly. So Basil's grandparents rightly fled to the forests of Pontus for seven years, and Athanasius rightly hid until the storm passed.
stances.quote: the law of martyrdom alike forbids us voluntarily to go to meet it (in consideration for the persecutors, and for the weak) or to shrink from it if it comes upon us; for the former shows foolhardiness, the latter cowardice
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 43, Funeral Oration on Basil the Great
stances.context: Delivered about 381-382. The sentence introduces the flight of Basil's paternal grandparents (including Macrina the Elder) during the persecution of Maximinus: "They betook themselves to a thicket on the mountains of Pontus" for "about seven years, or a little more", which he praises as faithful and rewarded by God (the miraculous deer, sections 7-8). In Oration 21 (on Athanasius, about 379-380), section 21, he praises Athanasius, who "approved the wise counsel of Solomon that there is a time to every purpose" and "hid himself for a while, escaping during the time of war, to show himself when the time of peace came" (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310221.htm). His Oration 2, often called the "Defence of his Flight", is about fleeing ordination, not persecution; do not confuse the two.

stances.summary: An apostle bears whatever comes without wavering, but he does not go looking for danger. Paul escaped Damascus in a basket, not from cowardice, but to save himself for preaching.
stances.quote: These things are the part of an apostolic soul, to suffer so great things and yet in nothing to veer about, but to bear nobly whatever befalls; yet not to go out to meet dangers, nor to rush upon them.
stances.translation: J. Ashworth, revised by Talbot W. Chambers, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 12, 1889
stances.context: Preached at Antioch, probably about 392-397. Next sentence: "See for instance here, how he was content to evade the siege, by being let down through a window in a basket", "preserving himself for the Preaching". Homily 20 on Acts says of the same escape: "this was no cowardice: he preserved himself for the preaching" (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210120.htm). Homily 34 on Matthew, on Matthew 10:23: "He did not at all command them, when persecuted, to close with the enemy, but to fly", though he reads that verse as said for the period before the cross (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200134.htm). No full treatise on the question. When he was sent into exile in 403-404 he went quietly rather than resist; that was exile, not flight. See misattributions: a line on flight in the Catena Aurea under "Pseudo-Chrys." is not his.

stances.summary: Christians need not fear persecution, and they may step out of its way. When persecution scattered the first believers from Jerusalem, it spread the Gospel.
stances.quote: they should not fear, but may shun persecution. This we see the believers did in the beginning, when on a persecution arising in Jerusalem they were scattered throughout all Judea, and thus the season of tribulation was made the seedtime of the Gospel.
stances.translation: Catena Aurea vol. 1 (St Matthew) part 1, Oxford translation edited by John Henry Newman, J. H. Parker, 1841
stances.original: quod persecutionem timere non debeant, sed declinare. Quod quidem videmus in principio fecisse credentes, quando orta Jerosolymis persecutione, dispersi sunt in universam Judaeam, ut tribulationis occasio fieret Evangelii seminarium.
stances.work: Commentary on Matthew, as excerpted in Thomas Aquinas, Catena Aurea
stances.context: Jerome's commentary (398) is not in NPNF and the Migne scan found (Documenta Catholica Omnia PDF) has no text layer, so this is read in Aquinas's excerpt, which may abridge. The page is plain-text OCR with irregular spacing, so compare with whitespace normalised; do not strip "tags" from it, because a stray OCR "<" just before "Go not into the way" makes a tag-stripper delete the quotation (checked: the quotation is present verbatim once whitespace is collapsed). The excerpt begins "This must be referred to the time when the Apostles were sent to preach, when it was said to them, Go not into the way of the Gentiles", so like Tertullian he ties the verse to the apostles' first mission, but unlike Tertullian he treats shunning persecution as good. Latin from the Latin Catena OCR at https://archive.org/download/catenaaureainqua0000stho/catenaaureainqua0000stho_djvu.txt (spelling normalised; OCR prints "Ju- deam" and "E- vangelii"). He also praises a fugitive in his Life of Paul the First Hermit (about 375): in the Decian persecution the young Paul "fled to the mountain wilds to wait for the end of the persecution", and that flight began the first hermit's life (section 5, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3008.htm).

stances.summary: In the last persecution the Church will flee from city to city and hide in the wilderness, with only faith in Christ to shelter her, as the Lord told those in Judea to flee to the mountains.
stances.quote: during which the tyrant is to reign and persecute the Church, which flees from city to city
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written about 200. Weak evidence: this is prophecy about Antichrist's reign (on Revelation 12:6), not a rule for present persecutions, though it pictures flight as the Church's proper course, protected by "the two wings of the great eagle, that is to say, the faith of Jesus Christ". Chapter 62 then cites Matthew 24:16, "flee into the mountains". Do not quote further in this sentence from newadvent: its text misprints "concealment" as "conceal-meat". Authorship of works under Hippolytus's name is debated, but this treatise is usually accepted as his.

stances.summary: When you can escape danger, escape. Refusing to, when escape is possible, is tempting God, and Christ and Paul both fled. But a pastor may not run if his people stay behind and still need him. Then love means staying.
stances.quote: not from want of faith in God did he thus escape, but because not to escape, when this escape was possible, would have been tempting God.
stances.translation: Richard Stothert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 4, 1887
stances.context: About 400. The "he" is Paul, let down over the Damascus wall in a basket. Same section: "it was not because the Saviour was unable to protect His disciples that He told them, When you are persecuted in one city, flee to another," and Christ Himself fled to Egypt, showing men "that they should not tempt God when they have any means in their power of escaping threatened danger". THE CLERGY EXCEPTION, Letter 228 to Bishop Honoratus (428 or 429, as the Vandals invaded; NPNF 1 vol. 1, J. G. Cunningham, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102228.htm): lay people who want to move to fortified places "are not to be forbidden"; a minister "specially sought for by persecutors, let him by all means flee from one city to another, provided that the Church is not hereby deserted"; but where the people remain and need the ministers, a bishop who flees is "the hireling who cares not for the sheep". He cites Athanasius's flight as a rightful one. He approves a bishop's saying that if we may flee persecution we may flee barbarians, but calls it "applicable only to those who are not confined by the obligations of ecclesiastical office". Not a change of mind, a qualification.

stances.summary: I will never willingly leave my church, though force may drag me out. I will not fight back, but I will not run. Christ wills to suffer in His servants, as He showed Peter when Peter tried to leave Rome.
stances.quote: I ought not, I cannot resist in any other way; but to fly and forsake the Church is not my way; lest any one should suppose I did so from fear of some heavier punishment.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: Sermon against Auxentius on the Giving Up of the Basilicas
stances.context: Preached in Milan in 386, while imperial troops loyal to the Arian empress Justina surrounded the basilica and the bishop had been ordered "to go hence, whither I would". Section 2 begins: "I will never willingly desert you, though if force is used, I cannot meet it." Section 1: "the wish to desert the Church had never entered my mind". Scope: this is a bishop refusing to abandon his people, and the threat was exile and violence rather than a death sentence; he does not discuss whether lay people may flee. Section 13 retells the "Quo vadis" story from the apocryphal Acts of Peter: Peter, persuaded by the Christians to withdraw from Rome, met Christ at the gate "coming to be crucified again", understood, "willingly returned" and was crucified. Section 15: "Christ's athlete needs not pleasant things but sufferings." Contrast Augustine, who allows flight to a hunted minister if others remain to serve the flock.

stances.summary: Bishop Maximus of Nola fled to the mountains in the persecution and kept his faith. His sick, cold, hungry exile was a real martyrdom, no gentler than the sword. Felix hid, and God hid him.
stances.quote: Meanwhile Maximus, sick in the lonely mountains, content to have fled the hands and the deathly faces of the executioners, was bearing martyrdom on a different cross, but no gentler one than if he had given his neck to the sword and his limbs to tortures or fires.
stances.translation: own rendering of the Latin, ed. W. von Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894
stances.original: Maximus interea solis in montibus aeger, contentus fugisse manus feraliaque ora carnificum, diversa at non leniore ferebat martyrium cruce, quam si ferro colla dedisset membraque tormentis aut ignibus
stances.work: Poem 15 (fourth Birthday Poem for St Felix)
stances.context: Written for Felix's feast in January 398. The only English (P. G. Walsh, 1975) is copyrighted, so the rendering is mine. The scan is OCR, so the Latin given here is corrected and will not match the page character for character: in these lines the OCR prints "camificum" for carnificum and "coUa" for colla, and inserts the edition's line number "200" before carnificum (and in 15.124 prints "fngatus" for fugatus). Search the page for "Maximus  interea  solis  in  montibus". Earlier (15.124-125) Maximus, "subita sed tempestate fugatus / non cedente fide petiit deserta locorum": driven off by the sudden storm, his faith not yielding, he made for the wilderness. At 15.339 Paulinus calls him "merito confessor", a confessor by merit. In Poem 16 (399), Felix hides and a spider's web over the gap in the wall fools the searchers: "sic ubi Christus adest nobis, et aranea muro est; / at cui Christus abest, et murus aranea fiet" (16.147-148), "so, where Christ is with us, even a spider's web is a wall; but where Christ is absent, a wall becomes a spider's web" (own rendering). Paulinus narrates rather than argues, but he plainly counts flight with faith kept as a kind of martyrdom, the same view as Athanasius (Defence of His Flight 17).

stances.summary: We do not praise those who hand themselves over, because the Gospel does not teach it. Polycarp withdrew from the city when his friends begged him, and waited to be handed over, as the Lord did.
stances.quote: Wherefore, brethren, we do not commend those who give themselves up [to suffering], seeing the Gospel does not teach so to do.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.work: The Martyrdom of Polycarp (letter of the Church of Smyrna)
stances.context: Written soon after Polycarp's death (about 155-160); the oldest martyr account outside the New Testament. Not in the results pool. Chapter 4 tells of Quintus the Phrygian, who "forced himself and some others to come forward voluntarily", then lost his nerve at the sight of the beasts and sacrificed. Polycarp himself (ch. 5) "resolved to stay in the city", but "in deference to the wish of many, he was persuaded to leave it", and moved again when hunted (ch. 6); at the end he refused one last chance to escape, saying "The will of God be done" (ch. 7). Chapter 1: "he waited to be delivered up, even as the Lord had done". The square brackets are the translators'.

stances.summary: Do not try to save me. I want to die for God. If you use your influence to get me released, you do me harm, not good. Let me be food for the beasts, so I may reach Christ.
stances.quote: I write to the Churches, and impress on them all, that I shall willingly die for God, unless you hinder me. I beseech of you not to show an unseasonable good-will towards me.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 107-115, on his way to Rome as a condemned prisoner. Scope: he was already arrested, so the question for him was rescue, not flight; he asks the Roman Christians not to intercede for his release. He never says others must not flee or lays down a rule. But his refusal of escape is the most emphatic in early Christian writing: "Allow me to become food for the wild beasts" (ch. 4); "do not hinder me from living, do not wish to keep me in a state of death" (ch. 6); "I am eager to die" (ch. 7). This is the middle-recension text translated in ANF (the one accepted as genuine).

splits_fathers: Lopsided toward agree. From Clement and Origen through Cyprian, Peter of Alexandria, Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine and Paulinus, the mainstream read Matthew 10:23 ("when they persecute you in this city, flee into another") as a real permission, often a command, and pointed to Christ's flight to Egypt and Paul's basket. The same writers condemned the opposite extreme, handing yourself over (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4, Clement Stromata 4.4 and 4.10, Peter canon 9, Cyprian's last letter, Gregory of Nazianzus Oration 43.6). The shared middle rule: do not volunteer, do not deny, flee if you can, confess if caught. Real voices on the other side exist but are few: Tertullian in his Montanist years (a whole treatise, reversing his earlier view), Ignatius (refusing rescue in his own case), and Ambrose (refusing, as bishop, to leave his flock). Antony stood openly without volunteering. Augustine drew the line at pastors: flight is right unless people who stay behind still need you. So among the Fathers the claim mainly separates Tertullian, Ignatius and Ambrose from nearly everyone else.
splits_people_today: Mostly agree, across Christians and others. Fleeing religious persecution is widely seen as legitimate (refugee law is built on it), and few ordinary people would call it wrong or faithless to escape if you can. A minority would disagree or hesitate: Christians with a strong martyrdom ethic, and many who feel that leaders, pastors or missionaries should stay with their people whatever the cost (a live question in places like northern Nigeria, Iraq or Syria). So the plain claim is one-sided today and one-sided among the Fathers; it will mainly pick out players who side with Tertullian. A version with more real split in both groups is the Augustine and Ambrose question: "A pastor should stay with his people in danger even if it will cost his life", or the bolder "It is better to stay and bear witness than to hide". Most people today and most Fathers say it is wrong to seek out martyrdom, so an item like "It can be right to hand yourself over to die for your faith" would split only a small fringe.

misattributions.line: Christians, when persecution makes it necessary, should not be ashamed to fly.
misattributions.attributed_to: John Chrysostom (via the Catena Aurea, on Matthew 2:13)
misattributions.truth: The Catena Aurea marks this "Pseudo-Chrys.": it comes from the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, an unfinished 5th-century commentary by an unknown (probably Arian) author long printed with Chrysostom's works. Chrysostom's genuine view is similar (Homily 25 on 2 Corinthians) but these words are not his.

misattributions.line: He who fled will fight again (He who fights and runs away lives to fight another day).
misattributions.attributed_to: sometimes cited as if Tertullian or a Christian maxim approving flight
misattributions.truth: A Greek proverb. Tertullian quotes it in On Flight in Persecution 10 as "that Greek versicle of worldly wisdom" only to reject it: "when will he who, as a fugitive, is a defeated man, be conqueror?"

misattributions.line: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.
misattributions.truth: A later paraphrase. His actual words (Apology 50, ANF 3) are "The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed."

misattributions.line: Domine, quo vadis? (Lord, where are You going?) spoken by Peter fleeing Rome.
misattributions.attributed_to: often assumed to be in the Bible
misattributions.truth: The scene at the gate of Rome comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter (late 2nd century), not Scripture. Ambrose retells it as history in the Sermon against Auxentius 13. Peter asks "Lord, whither goest thou?" in John 13:36, but at the Last Supper, not in flight.

notes:
WHAT THE QUESTION REALLY SORTS. The famous early quarrel was whether flight is lawful at all (Tertullian against almost everyone). A second, quieter quarrel was about leaders: Tertullian (De Fuga 11), the Roman clergy writing to Carthage in 250 (their letter, Epistle 2 in ANF numbering, says Cyprian withdrew "quite rightly" but then quotes the hireling who "leaves the sheep, and flees"), Ambrose, and Augustine's Letter 228 all say a shepherd has special reasons to stay. Most of the "agree" voices also condemned volunteering, which the Montanists and later the Donatist Circumcellions admired.

BEST LINES FOR A REVEAL: Cyprian, "He is not alone, whose companion in flight Christ is" (Epistle 55 ANF, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050655.htm). Origen, "when it is in our power to avoid it, not to do so is rash." Tertullian, "who will flee from persecution, but he who fears? Who will fear, but he who has not loved?" Augustine, "not to escape, when this escape was possible, would have been tempting God." Ambrose, "to fly and forsake the Church is not my way". Paulinus on the spider's web (own rendering, in his entry).

CHANGES OF MIND: Tertullian (permitted in To His Wife 1.3, condemned in On Flight, about a decade later). Origen as a teenager rushed toward martyrdom and his mother hid his clothes (Eusebius, Church History 6.2); as a grown teacher he called needless exposure "rash and headstrong". Cyprian fled in 250 and stayed in 258, but on one consistent principle (a time to withdraw, a time to confess).

LEADS NOT VERIFIED (no stance entered): Basil's Homily on the martyr Gordius, a soldier who withdrew to the desert and then walked into the theatre to confess, praised by Basil (Greek in PG 31; no pre-1929 English found; could give Basil a volunteer-leaning stance if someone reads the Greek). Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Gregory the Wonderworker, which reportedly says Gregory led his flock into flight in the Decian persecution (Greek in PG 46; only English is Slusser, Fathers of the Church 98, 1998, copyrighted). Hilary's comment on Matthew 10:23 (seen only in the Catena Aurea) is allegorical, about the Gospel passing from Judea to the Gentiles, so no stance. Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule 2.4, says bad pastors "fly when the wolf comes if they hide themselves under silence": that is about silence, not physical flight, so no stance. Justin Martyr, Second Apology 4, is about why Christians do not kill themselves, not about flight. Perpetua's own diary (Passion 4.5; ANF chapter 1, section 3) says Saturus "had subsequently delivered himself up freely on our account", since he was not there when they were arrested, but she states no rule. Moses the Black stayed and Arsenius fled when barbarians raided Scetis, but those raids were not persecution for faith. The Montanist oracle Tertullian quotes (De Fuga 9: "seek not to die on bridal beds ... but to die the martyr's death") is anonymous prophecy.

COPYING CAUTIONS: newadvent inserts Bible references inline (for example "Matthew 10:23") and has typos in places (Hippolytus: "conceal-meat"; Epistle 55: dashes dropped, "firstthe"). The quotations above were chosen to avoid those spots. The archive.org texts are OCR with irregular spacing; normalise whitespace before checking.
